u.src: What makes a composite system a particle?

p.src: A string is extended and will be modeled by many coupled pieces. In what sense can one of its quantum states nevertheless be a particle? Pointlikeness cannot be the decisive criterion. Protons and neutrons are composite. Electrons and photons are accompanied by quantum-field dressing even though no intrinsic substructure has been resolved. A classical geometric point surrounded by nothing is not the right image of a quantum excitation.

p.src: The useful criterion is spectral isolation. Put the rest energy on a vertical axis and ask how much energy is required to reach another internal state. An electron has no experimentally accessible tower of electron excitations just above it. A proton does have resonances, but the first ones cost a few hundred MeV, a substantial fraction of the proton mass. Those states are separated enough to be individually identifiable.

p.src: This criterion turns the philosophical question into a calculation. Quantize the string, find its internal energy levels, and inspect their spacing. If the first excited string state lies near the Planck scale while the observed ground state is light, the gap exceeds present accelerator energies by more than twenty orders of magnitude. The string then behaves as an elementary particle throughout the accessible regime.

p.src: The essential conclusion is already visible. Successive levels are separated by finite gaps, and each has a finite multiplicity. The quantized string is therefore particle-like by the spectral criterion that distinguished it from coffee, gas, or an ordinary violin string. Later we shall determine which states are physically welcome and which pathologies must be removed.

u.src: Why open-string interactions produce closed strings
en: Why open-string interactions produce closed strings

p.src: An open string has two endpoints. Its elementary interactions join and split strings. In the hadronic picture one may imagine a quark at one end and an antiquark at the other; their annihilation joins two string segments. The fundamental strings of interest later need not carry that literal hadronic endpoint interpretation, but the local joining rule remains.

p.src: Now let one open string fluctuate until its own endpoints approach one another. Locally, an endpoint cannot know that the other endpoint belongs to the same string rather than a different one. If endpoints may join at all, they may join here, producing a closed loop.

p.src: Thus a theory may contain closed strings without open strings, but an interacting theory with open strings cannot consistently avoid closed strings. This asymmetry is the important prediction. The spectral identifications will be developed later, but the destination is already visible: massless open-string states often supply gauge particles such as photons, while the closed-string spectrum contains a massless spin-two state, the graviton. Closed strings, and therefore gravity, are not an optional decoration once string theory is interacting.
